questions.q: What distinguishes an American option from a European option?
options: American options can only be traded in the United States
American options can be exercised at any time up to and including expiration; European options can only be exercised at expiration
American options have no strike price
European options always pay a higher premium
questions.explain: The 'American' and 'European' labels refer to exercise timing, not geography. American options allow early exercise, which adds value and requires numerical methods like trees to price correctly.

questions.q: What does an Asian option's payoff depend on?
options: The stock price at a single moment, like a vanilla option
The average price of the underlying over a specified window of time
Whether the stock touches a barrier level
The interest rate at expiration only
questions.explain: Asian options pay off based on the average underlying price over a window, which reduces exposure to a single-day price spike and makes the option harder to manipulate near expiration.

questions.q: What is the difference between a knock-out and a knock-in barrier option?
options: A knock-out starts active and ceases to exist if the barrier is touched; a knock-in starts inactive and only becomes active if the barrier is touched
A knock-out can never expire worthless; a knock-in always expires worthless
They are two names for the exact same structure
A knock-out only applies to puts, and a knock-in only applies to calls
questions.explain: Knock-out options can be extinguished by touching the barrier, while knock-in options require the barrier to be touched before they come into existence at all.

questions.q: Why do exotic options like Asian, barrier, American, and lookback options generally require numerical methods rather than a closed-form formula like Black-Scholes?
options: Because they are illegal to price with formulas
Because their payoffs depend on the entire price path or on an early-exercise decision, rather than on the stock price at a single future point in time
Because they never have a strike price
Because closed-form formulas only work for interest rate products
questions.explain: Black-Scholes's closed form works because the vanilla payoff depends on one number at one point in time. Path dependence or early-exercise flexibility breaks that structure, which is why trees, Monte Carlo simulation, or finite-difference PDE methods are used instead.

questions.q: Which numerical method is most naturally suited to pricing path-dependent payoffs like Asian or lookback options?
options: Put-call parity
Monte Carlo simulation — simulating many random price paths and averaging the discounted payoffs
A single evaluation of the Black-Scholes formula
Reading the implied volatility off a vanilla option
questions.explain: Monte Carlo simulation naturally handles path-dependent payoffs because it simulates the full trajectory of the underlying price under the risk-neutral measure, then computes and averages the payoff across many simulated paths.
